title: Control Plane Split and Delegated mTLS: Handoff + Multi-region Routing Notes
content:
Purpose
This doc captures a proposed pattern for splitting the control plane across global and regional domains and a delegated mTLS handoff pattern for ingress/egress paths in multi-region deployments. Focus: operational safety, predictable failover, and limiting blast radius during cert rotation or region failures.

Scope and assumptions
- Applies to Redwood Private and Dedicated customers that opt into multi-region redundancy.
- We assume an edge/router layer in each region (cloud-provided LB or neutral edge), regional control plane presence (regional controllers), and a global control plane for policy and catalog.
- Service mesh dataplane will be Envoy-based initially; sidecarless/ebpf options are evaluated as alternatives.

Goals
- Keep control-plane decisions local when possible to reduce cross-region latency for routing and scaling decisions.
- Ensure mTLS identity chaining across ingress->regional-proxy->service mesh with minimal key exposure and clear rotation paths.
- Provide deterministic routing policies (latency-aware, cost-aware, tenant-affinity) and safe fallbacks for region failures.

Key definitions
- Global control plane: authoritative catalog, model versions, global rollout directives, and cross-region policy.
- Regional control plane: local decisioning (routing priority, autoscale signals, hot retry policies), health aggregation for local endpoints.
- Delegated mTLS handoff: edge or regional proxy proves client identity to downstream proxies/services via short-lived certs or token exchange mediated by local CA/Spiffe agent.

Proposed architecture (high level)
1) Edge/Global: Public ingress terminates TLS at edge LB. Edge performs initial authn/authz (API keys / JWT introspection). Edge then performs a delegated identity handoff to the regional boundary.
2) Regional boundary (regional-proxy): runs in-region Envoy (or envoy fleet) with SPIFFE/SPIRE agent. The regional-proxy holds a regional CA-signed SVIDs for downstream traffic and issues ephemeral certs for per-request or per-connection use.
3) Regional control plane: syncs with global control plane for policies and rollout metadata but owns routing priority/local affinity/scale decisions.
4) Mesh dataplane: services accept mTLS from regional-proxy and enforce SPIFFE identities for authorization. Sidecars validate SVIDs and apply local RBAC.

Delegated mTLS handoff pattern details
- Why: Avoid passing long-lived edge keys deep into the mesh and reduce cross-region certificate validations.
- Flow: client -> edge TLS (client cert optional) -> edge authenticates client and issues a short-lived token bound to the request (signed JWT) -> regional-proxy redeems token with local SPIRE agent for an ephemeral SVID (mTLS cert) -> regional-proxy mTLS to downstream service.
- Rotations: regional CA keys rotate independently on a region cadence; the regional control plane coordinates a rolling rotation across proxies to avoid simultaneous mass-renegotiation.
- Verification: services only trust regionally-issued SVIDs plus explicit global roots for cross-region mutual-comms.

Control plane split considerations
- Data flow: keep health checks and autoscale signals local. Global control plane should not be in the critical path for traffic shaping decisions.
- Consistency: model/version metadata should be eventually-consistent; clients routed to a region must see a consistent model version snapshot for the duration of a request. Achieve this via version id checks on the regional caches.
- Failover: on global-control-plane loss, regionals continue operating using last-known policies and fall back to safe defaults for new deployments.

Routing policies and multi-region decisioning
- Primary selectors: latency, region-affinity (customer data locality), cost (spot vs reserved), and capacity headroom.
- Policy precedence: tenant-configured affinity > latency > cost > capacity-preference.
- Traffic shaping knobs: per-tenant max QPS per region, burst tokens, circuit-breaker thresholds, and slow-start for rollouts.
- Canary across regions: use global control plane to initiate cross-region canaries with progressive traffic shifts using explicit delegations to regional controllers.

Ingress/egress patterns and egress governance
- Ingress: edge -> regional-proxy -> service mesh. Edge enforces coarse ACLs and quota, regionals enforce identity and fine-grained RBAC.
- Egress: prefer region-local egress gateways for outbound third-party calls to reduce cross-region bandwidth and tax. Egress gateways perform egress mTLS for external endpoints when required and NAT consolidation for auditability.
- Outbound retries: avoid cross-region retries on user-facing requests; limit to region-local pools then escalate to cross-region fallback.

Service mesh specifics and alternatives
- Sidecar vs sidecarless:
  - Sidecar (Envoy): well-known semantics, per-pod identity, rich L7 controls. Cost: CPU/memory and more TLS handshakes.
  - Sidecarless (eBPF + user-space proxies): lower overhead, faster path for short-lived workloads, but higher operational complexity and fewer maturity features for L7.
- Recommendation: start with Envoy sidecars, optimize hotspots with eBPF-based path for high-throughput stateless inference nodes only.

Observability and tracing
- Correlate edge request id -> regional id -> service span. Propagate a single request-id and an identity-chain header for postmortem identity mapping.
- Telemetry: expose mTLS handshake metrics, handshake failures, certificate rotation events, cross-region latency heatmaps.
- Alerting: mTLS negotiation failure rate > 0.5% over 5m triggers incident; regional control plane divergence > 30s triggers controlled governor mode.

Operational playbooks (high-level)
- Cert rotation:
  1) Stage rotation in a canary regional-proxy group (10%).
  2) Monitor handshake/error metrics for 15m.
  3) Roll regionally in waves with staggered TTLs.
- Region failover:
  1) Regional control-plane detects loss and marks region degraded.
  2) Global control plane reweights traffic according to failover policy and notifies regionals.
  3) If regional services are unreachable for 2 minutes, cut traffic and notify SRE with automatic rollback tokens.
- Emergency rollback: maintain an immutable global safe-policy that can be forced via API key to route all traffic away from a region.

Security and compliance notes
- Key management: regional CA private keys stored in HSM or cloud KMS. Use envelope encryption for local SPIRE agents.
- Auditing: every delegated token issuance and SVID redemption must be logged to immutable audit storage with tenant and request id.
- Data locality: tenant-affinity + ingress ACLs enforce that requests tied to regulated tenant stay in permitted regions by default.

Outstanding questions / tradeoffs
- How aggressive should regional autonomy be for autoscaling decisions? (latency gains vs global consistency)
- Token vs certificate handoff: per-request JWT redemption costs vs per-connection ephemeral certs; we need load tests to size redemption throughput.
- Sidecarless operational model: how quickly can we instrument eBPF path and replicate Envoy features needed for RBAC?

Immediate next steps / action items
- ENG-4821: prototype token-to-SVID redemption path with a regional SPIRE agent (owner: Marco Li).
- Load test: simulate 20k QPS ingress with per-request token redemptions, measure redemption p95 and CPU cost (owner: Ethan Morales).
- RFC: write short RFC for regional control plane responsibilities and failure modes (owner: Priya Shah).

Notes and references
- See GH PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/284 (initial envoy filters for token exchange).
- Confluence draft: platform/control-plane-split (sync with product on rollout requirements).

Bottom line
Delegated mTLS with a split control plane buys us lower cross-region latency for routing decisions and a smaller blast radius for key material, at the cost of added operational complexity (token redemption, regional CA rotation). Prioritize a small prototype and load tests to validate token redemption scale and then iterate on a canary rollout model for cert rotations.
